                                            I.     INTRODUCTION

          Kevin Kennedy (“Mr. Kennedy”), retired professional engineer, landowner, and pro se

intervenor, respectfully files this Brief on Remand of Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 to

the State Office of Administrative Hearings ("SOAH") Administrative Law Judges ("ALJs")

regarding Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC’s (“Oncor’s”) and LCRA Transmission

Services Corporation’s (“LCRA’s”) (collectively, “Applicants”) application to amend a

certificate of convenience and necessity (“CCN”) for the Bell County East to Big Hill 765-kV

transmission line (“59475”). The Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) remanded

only those two issues to SOAH for further consideration.

          The 59475 proceedings were consolidated by SOAH to the extent necessary to address

common need issues with Applicants’ Big Hill to Sand Lake 765-kV transmission line

(“59182”), so this brief addresses need and consumer savings issues in both 59475 and 59182. 1

          The ALJs ordered briefing on the existing evidentiary record and directed that factual

assertions include specific record citations. This brief therefore does not ask the ALJs to reopen

the record to new evidence. It asks the ALJs to answer the two questions the Commission

returned to them based on the evidence already admitted. 2 3

                                                     II.     SUMMARY

           The remand asks why these proposed facilities would be recommended, not whether

ERCOT supports a statewide transmission plan. Applicants have not connected the portfolio

results to the project-specific reliability necessity and estimated congestion savings required by

Issues 11 and 13.


           The later RTP evidence does not cure that problem. The 2024 RTP's 765-kV start case

already included all three Permian Basin 765-kV import paths. Mr. Gurley testified that he was

not aware of a study that isolated each line independently because the lines were studied

together. That is evidence of portfolio-level planning. It is not the same thing as proof that this

specific CCN facility is necessary to satisfy a particular reliability standard. 4 5


           That failure exists even if the PBRP is assumed to be technically correct, but the record

adds a second problem. The PBRP and the contemporaneous 2024 RTP were built for different

purposes and with materially different system assumptions. The PBRP itself acknowledges

approximately 59,400 MW of additional statewide demand identified for the 2024 RTP by 2030,

while its Appendix A.1 lists only approximately 17,170 MW of generation added to the PBRP

study cases. Those differences do not prove the PBRP is invalid. They do mean Applicants

needed record evidence showing that the differences do not materially affect the long-distance

transfer need attributed to Import Path 2. The existing record does not supply that reconciliation. 6


           Issue 13 presents the same project-specific problem. Applicants originally told the ALJs

that this Project was not justified on economic criteria. The PFD found that Applicants did not

                                  III.    PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 11

               Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability
               standards?

       A. The question on remand is whether this facility is necessary, not whether ERCOT
           favors a 765-kV portfolio.

                The Applicants' strongest evidence proves a broader proposition than Issue 11 asks.

       The PBRP states that its reliability assessments were performed based on NERC Reliability

       Standard TPL-001-5.1, ERCOT Protocols, and ERCOT Planning Criteria. That shows what

       criteria ERCOT says it used in the study. It does not by itself establish that the absence of

       Bell County East to Big Hill causes a violation of any identified requirement. 11

                The Commission remanded because the PFD did not answer that precise question.

       Chairman Gleeson wrote that Issue 11 asks whether the facilities are 'in fact necessary' to

       meet state or federal reliability standards, not how Applicants characterize the project. That

       distinction controls the remand analysis. A finding that a large plan improves transfer

       capability, system strength, or operational flexibility is not a substitute for a finding that this

       particular facility is necessary to comply with a reliability standard. 12

                PURA also makes the distinction consequential. The Commission may grant a

       certificate only if it finds the certificate necessary for the service, accommodation,

       convenience, or safety of the public. If an ERCOT transmission project is not necessary to

       meet state or federal reliability standards, PURA requires additional economic criteria that

       include consumer cost and congestion savings.13

13

       B. Applicants did not prove project-specific necessity even if the PBRP is assumed
          correct.

               This is the first and most important point. Mr. Kennedy does not need the ALJs to

      find that the PBRP was invalid in order to answer “no” to Issue 11. Assume for purposes of

      argument that every PBRP input was proper, every modeled contingency was correct, and

      every portfolio recommendation was technically sound. Applicants still had to prove that the

      proposed Bell County East to Big Hill facilities are necessary to meet a state or federal

      reliability standard.

               They did not.

               The admitted record contains portfolio-level studies. It contains ERCOT conclusions

      about the three Permian import paths combined, the broader 765-kV core plan, and Far West

      transfer needs. But Mr. Gurley testified that he was not aware of a study that isolated each

      import path independently because the lines were studied together. That concession

      identifies a critical limitation in the proof Applicants presented. A study showing that a group

      of facilities performs well does not establish that this particular Import Path 2 facility must be

      built to avoid a reliability violation.14


          Mr. Kennedy does not contend that NERC requires one prescribed study format or that

facilities in an interconnected system must operate independently. Gurley attributed the

combined study to NERC contingency requirements and then pointed to the GTC exit plan as

requiring all of the lines in 2030. Those answers deserve consideration. But neither an assumed

need for all lines nor a portfolio recommendation identifies the particular reliability requirement




14
     Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:14-45:17 (Gurley Cross) (Item No. 6137).


KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Brief on Remand of Issues 11 and 13                                  Page 8 of 32
 that cannot be met without Import Path 2. A removal case or other supported analysis connecting

the proposed facilities to that requirement is still missing from Applicants’ showing. 15

               Applicants therefore fail Issue 11 on their own evidence before any modeling

      criticism is considered. The engineering questions discussed below compound that failure.

      They are not a substitute for the project-specific proof that is already missing.


      C. The unresolved differences between the PBRP and the 2024 RTP compound
           Applicants' failure of proof.

               Mr. Kennedy and fellow intervenor Mr. John Burrow have repeatedly identified a

      separate engineering concern in the existing record. The PBRP and 2024 RTP were

      developed during overlapping planning periods, but they were not the same case. Different

      studies may properly use different assumptions. The issue here is what Applicants proved

      about the effect of those differences on the roughly 400-mile Import Path 2 whose purpose is

      to move power across large portions of the ERCOT system.

               The PBRP used the final 2023 RTP case as its starting case and constructed its 2030

      and 2038 steady-state cases by updating transmission, generation, and loads for the West and

      Far West study condition. The same PBRP acknowledged that TDSP forecasts for the 2024

      RTP identified approximately 59,400 MW of additional demand across the ERCOT system

      that would need to be served by 2030. Appendix A.1 of the PBRP lists just approximately

      17,170 MW of generation added to its study base cases. These figures describe different

      quantities: additional forecast demand and generation added to particular study cases.

      Subtracting one from the other does not establish a generation shortfall or a defective model.




15

        The relevant question is whether Applicants demonstrated how the differing system

       assumptions affect the claimed transfer need and performance of Import Path 2. 16 17 18

                Those facts do not authorize the ALJs to declare the PBRP model defective. The

       record is closed, and SOAH correctly declined to conduct the independent investigation Mr.

       Kennedy requested because SOAH lacks self-initiating investigative authority. The proper

       evidentiary consequence is narrower. The record contains a material, unreconciled question

       about how the PBRP system assumptions compare with the contemporaneous statewide

       planning assumptions that ERCOT used elsewhere. 19 This issue limits what ERCOT’s

       recommendations can establish about these particular facilities. Giving ERCOT’s

       recommendation great weight does not turn a conclusion about a portfolio into conclusive

       proof of the necessity of each facility within it.20

                That question matters because Import Path 2 is not a local radial line serving a single

       load pocket. Applicants describe the import paths as facilities that transfer power between

       West Texas and other parts of ERCOT. A material change in load or generation in the

       supposed source regions can change the amount and direction of power available to move

       west. Applicants therefore needed evidence connecting the PBRP assumptions to the claimed

       necessity and performance of Bell County East to Big Hill.

                The admitted discovery evidence reinforces that gap. Applicants stated that the STEP

       and Permian Basin load cases are separate and distinct, that they did not know the total MW

       of Central Texas data-center load included in the ERCOT load forecast used to justify the

        Permian projects, and that neither Oncor nor ERCOT studies parse out the Central Texas

       region's net generation position. Those answers do not prove the PBRP wrong. They show

       that the Applicants did not supply the reconciliation necessary to eliminate the modeling

       concern from this CCN record.21

                   The result is cumulative. First, Applicants did not prove project-specific necessity

       even assuming the PBRP is correct. Second, the record contains unresolved engineering

       questions concerning the model on which Applicants principally rely. The second problem

       makes the first one harder to overcome, not easier.


       D. The PBRP did not establish a 765-kV reliability necessity for Import Path 2.

                   The starting point is ERCOT's own PBRP. For 2030, ERCOT considered only a 345-

       kV import path option. For 2038, ERCOT evaluated the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV import

       path options. The PBRP separately states that the 765-kV import path option was evaluated

       for the 2038 Permian Basin region load level. It also anticipated a later systemwide EHV

       study of 2030 needs and possible substitution of EHV lines for the 2030 345-kV paths. That

       possibility must be distinguished from a project-specific necessity finding in the PBRP

       itself.22

                   That chronology matters because the Applicants now ask the ALJs to find that Bell

       County East to Big Hill is presently necessary as a reliability project. Mr. Gurley's rebuttal

       testimony confirms that the spreadsheet attached to ERCOT's December 2024 sequencing

       letter listed 2038 as the year when the reliability need began to appear for all three 765-kV

       import paths.23

                Mr. Gurley also testified that the later 2024 RTP showed Import Path 2 in the '765-kV

      Core Plan needed in 2030' and that the 2025 RTP included all three import paths in the 2030

      and 2031 study cases. That later evidence is relevant and should not be ignored. But it does

      not erase the fact that the PBRP relied upon in this Application evaluated 765 kV for 2038,

      not 2030. Nor does it answer whether Bell County East to Big Hill, standing alone, was the

      facility necessary to eliminate a specific reliability violation.24


      E. The later RTP studies began with the three Permian import paths already in the
           765-kV case.

               The 2024 RTP is useful evidence of ERCOT's system planning judgment, but its

      construction limits what can be inferred about this individual project. The 765-kV start case

      already incorporated all local projects needed by 2030 in the PBRP together with all three

      Permian Basin 765-kV import paths.

               ERCOT described its method plainly: it began by developing a holistic 765-kV plan

      and then identified the critical components, or core plan, needed by 2030. That is a

      legitimate system-planning approach. But it is not an independent before-and-after test of

      Bell County East to Big Hill. If the project is present in the starting case, the study may show

      the performance of a system containing the project. It does not, without a corresponding

      removal case or other supported project-specific analysis, establish what reliability violation

      appears because this project is absent. 25

                    The same limitation carries into the 2025 RTP. The entire 765-kV STEP was

           included in the 2030 and 2031 starting base cases, and ERCOT reported that it did not see

           a need to remove any element. That supports ERCOT's continued support for the

            portfolio. It still does not identify an isolated reliability violation caused by the absence

           of this line.26


      F. The record contains no independent study isolating Bell County East to Big Hill.

               This is not speculation. Mr. Gurley was asked whether a study isolated each line

      independently. He answered that he was not aware of such a study because the lines were

      studied together.

               That answer goes to the heart of Issue 11. The Applicants seek a CCN for a specific

      facility. The remanded issue asks whether the proposed facilities are necessary to meet state

      or federal reliability standards. Yet the principal planning evidence evaluates grouped

      facilities and broad system configurations. The absence of an independent isolation study,

      together with the failure to identify the specific reliability requirement that cannot otherwise

      be met, leaves unproven that Import Path 2 is the facility that must be built to avoid a

      reliability violation.


      G. Package-wide GTC and transfer evidence does not identify the particular reliability
           violation that requires this facility.

               Applicants also rely on Far West Generic Transmission Constraint evidence. Mr.

      Martin's rebuttal identifies six transmission projects in the North to Far West GTC exit

      strategy, and the table lists the 'Permian Basin 765 kV Import Paths' collectively with a 2030

      expected in-service year. That evidence supports a conclusion that ERCOT sees the three

      PBRP import paths as part of a larger exit strategy. It does not identify which violation, if

      any, is cured by Bell County East to Big Hill, or establish that the same standard cannot be

      met through the remainder of the portfolio or another configuration. 27

               Martin also identifies NERC FAC-011-4 in discussing operating limits and calls

      Import Path 2 critical to the GTC exit strategy, even if planned local generation materializes.

      Mr. Kennedy’s point is not that the witnesses named no standard or described no reliability

      risk. FAC-011-4 addresses the methodology for determining and assessing system operating

      limits. Applicants still must connect an applicable requirement and the studied operating

      conditions to the necessity of these proposed facilities. A conclusion that all three import

      paths are critical to ERCOT’s chosen exit strategy does not, by itself, supply that missing

      analysis.28

              The Applicants' admitted discovery responses expose the same gap on the eastern

      source side of the line. Applicants stated that they do not know the total MW of Central

      Texas data-center load included in the forecast used to justify the Permian projects, cannot

      determine precise customer loads that will be served by east-west power flow from this line,

      and that neither Oncor nor ERCOT studies parse out Central Texas's net generation position.

      Those answers do not prove the line will not carry power west. They do show that the record

      does not quantify the source-side surplus or project-specific east-west delivery that would

      connect this particular facility to the asserted Permian import need. 29


      H. The load sensitivity evidence may support ERCOT's broader reliability concern,
          but it still does not prove project-specific necessity.

              Mr. Kennedy does not ignore the evidence that cuts the other way. In the 2024 RTP

      reduced-load sensitivity, ERCOT reduced officer-letter load from more than 31 GW to less

      than 16 GW and reported that the key reliability needs remained similar. That is meaningful

       evidence that ERCOT's broader transmission need is not wholly dependent on every

      forecasted large load materializing.30

               But the sensitivity was still performed within a system-planning framework in which

      the Permian import path was included. The same report states that the reduced-load

      sensitivity costs for the 345-kV and 765-kV plans included the Permian Basin Reliability

      Import Path. The sensitivity therefore strengthens the case that ERCOT expects major

      system upgrades under lower load. It does not answer the narrower remand question of

      whether Bell County East to Big Hill itself is necessary to meet a specific state or federal

      reliability standard.31

      I. The proper answer to Issue 11 is that project-specific reliability necessity was not
          established.

               The record supports a finding that ERCOT recommends the 765-kV portfolio, that it

      expects major Permian load growth, that it sees reliability benefits from large import

      capability, and that later RTPs retained the three paths. But the same record shows that the

      PBRP's 765-kV evaluation was for 2038, that later 765-kV RTP cases began with the three

      paths already installed, and that Gurley did not identify a study isolating each line

      independently.

               That is not enough to make the finding Issue 11 requires. The Applicants did not

      identify the specific state or federal reliability violation that occurs because Bell County East

      to Big Hill is absent, and the admitted studies do not isolate this facility to demonstrate that

      causal link. Issue 11 should therefore be answered: No, the existing record does not

      establish that the proposed facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability

      standards.

                                  IV.     PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 13

               What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the
               proposed transmission facilities considering both current and future expected
               congestion levels and the ability of the proposed transmission facilities to reduce those
               congestion levels?

       A. Applicants originally told the ALJs this Project was not justified on economic
           criteria.

                Applicants' original answer to Issue 13 could not have been clearer: 'This Project is

       needed to address reliability issues and establish additional load-serving capacity and is not

       justified based on economic criteria.' That was the case Applicants chose to present. That

       statement appears in Applicants’ Initial Post-Hearing Brief, in their answer to Issue 13. 32

                The PFD reflected the resulting record. It found that Applicants did not submit the

       estimated cost of the facilities to consumers or the estimated congestion cost savings to

       consumers that may result from the proposed transmission facilities, and that the record

       contained no evidence quantifying either. 33

                The remand does not reopen the record. Applicants therefore cannot replace the

       missing project-specific economic case with a new study. They can only point to economic

       evidence already admitted. The question is whether that evidence actually answers Issue 13

       for Bell County East to Big Hill.


       B. The economic evidence Applicants now rely upon analyzes the whole 765-kV plan,
           not Import Path 2 standing alone.

                Applicants' Directory relies heavily on Exhibit JG-4, ERCOT's comparison of the

       345-kV plan and the Texas 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan. But that study is

        not a Bell County East to Big Hill economic analysis. The 765-kV start case incorporated the

       three Permian Basin 765-kV import paths together with the other projects in the larger plan. 34

                Mr. Gurley's testimony again supplies the critical limitation: he was not aware of a

       study that isolated each line independently because the lines were studied together. Without

       a comparison that removes Bell County East to Big Hill while holding the rest of the system

       constant, or another supported allocation of the benefits, the resulting system-wide savings

       cannot be assigned to Import Path 2 on this record.


       C. ERCOT's 2034 consumer energy cost results do not show superior consumer
